abstract: Spatial subcellular distributions of lysosomes are intricately coupled with their functional heterogeneities, yet how neurons preferentially allocate distinct subtypes of lysosomes between the soma and axons remains largely unknown. Here, we discover that the axon initial segment (AIS) may function as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint by actively sorting lysosomes based on their functional states. Central to this checkpoint is MCF2L, a specific lysosome-associated protein enriched in AIS, that anchors clustered lysosomes at AIS via high-affinity binding to giant ankyrin-G (gAnkG, encoded by Ank3). Selective ablation of the MCF2L-gAnkG interaction accelerates disease progression in a mouse Parkinson's disease model. By clustering lysosomes, MCF2L restricts kinesin-mediated transport and regulates lysosomal positioning. In neurons, MCF2L-mediated lysosome clustering may act as a lysosomal quality-control checkpoint, by which less acidic (e.g., impaired) lysosomes are retained in AIS and functionally intact lysosomes are released for transport. Thus, AIS may impart neurons with a unique mechanism for axonal lysosome compartmentalization and quality control.
